blocks.text: Imagine building a house without a blueprint. In software engineering, requirements are your blueprint. How do you make sure they're clear and prioritized?

blocks.markdown: In software engineering, specifying and prioritizing requirements is crucial to the success of a project. A requirement must be clear, testable, and prioritized to ensure that the development team builds the right product. In this lesson, we will explore how to rewrite vague requirements to make them testable and how to prioritize requirements effectively.

blocks.title: Requirement
blocks.text: A requirement is a statement about a system's functionality or characteristics that must be met or possessed by the system to satisfy a contract, standard, specification, or other formally imposed document.

blocks.markdown: A common issue in software projects is vague requirements. A vague requirement is one that is open to interpretation and cannot be directly tested. To avoid this, requirements must be specified in a way that they can be tested. This means they should be clear, unambiguous, and measurable.

blocks.title: Rewriting a Vague Requirement
blocks.prompt: Consider the requirement: 'The system should be easy to use.' How can this be rewritten to be testable?

steps.text: Identify the vague term: 'easy to use'.
Define what 'easy to use' means in measurable terms. For example, 'The system should allow a new user to complete a task within 5 minutes without external help.'
Ensure the requirement can be tested. The rewritten requirement specifies a measurable time and condition that can be tested with users.

blocks.answer: The system should allow a new user to complete a task within 5 minutes without external help.

blocks.title: Testable Requirements
blocks.text: A requirement is testable if you can design a test to verify if the system meets the requirement.

blocks.markdown: Once requirements are specified clearly, they need to be prioritized. Prioritization helps in deciding which requirements to implement first, especially when resources are limited. Common prioritization techniques include MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have) and the Kano model.

rows: Critical requirements that are essential for the system to work.
Important requirements but not critical for the initial release.
Desirable requirements that can improve user experience.
Requirements that will not be implemented in this release but may be considered for the future.
blocks.caption: MoSCoW Prioritization Technique

blocks.title: Prioritizing Requirements
blocks.prompt: Given the following requirements for a new e-commerce platform, prioritize them using the MoSCoW technique: 1) Secure payment processing, 2) User reviews, 3) Mobile app support, 4) Social media integration.

steps.text: Identify critical requirements: Secure payment processing is essential for the platform to function, so it's a 'Must have'.
Determine important but not critical requirements: Mobile app support is important for user accessibility, so it's a 'Should have'.
Identify desirable features: User reviews enhance user experience, so it's a 'Could have'.
Consider future enhancements: Social media integration is nice to have but not essential, so it's a 'Won't have' for now.

blocks.answer: 1) Must have: Secure payment processing, 2) Should have: Mobile app support, 3) Could have: User reviews, 4) Won't have: Social media integration.

blocks.title: Cost of Late Requirement Defects
blocks.text: Finding a defect in requirements late in the development process can be costly. It may require redesign, reimplementation, and retesting, leading to increased time and budget.

points: Requirements must be clear, unambiguous, and testable.
Prioritization helps in managing resources effectively and delivering critical features first.
Late discovery of requirement defects can significantly increase project costs.
